{{Short description|American mathematician}}
{{infobox scientist/Wikidata | fetchwikidata=ALL}}
'''Richard Evan Schwartz''' (born August 11, 1966) is an American [[mathematician]] notable for his contributions to [[geometric group theory]] and to an area of [[mathematics]] known as [[Outer billiard|billiards]]. Geometric group theory is a relatively new area of mathematics beginning around the late 1980s<ref name="M. Gromov, 1987, pp. 75–263">[[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|M. Gromov]], ''Hyperbolic Groups'', in "Essays in Group Theory" (G. M. Gersten, ed.), MSRI Publ. 8, 1987, pp. 75–263.</ref> which explores finitely generated groups, and seeks connections between their algebraic properties and the geometric spaces on which these groups act. He has worked on what mathematicians refer to as ''[[Outer billiard|billiards]]'', which are [[dynamical system]]s based on a [[convex set|convex]] shape in a plane. He has explored geometric iterations involving [[polygons]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berger |first=Marcel |author-link=Marcel Berger |date=2005 |title=Dynamiser la géométrie élémentaire: introduction à des travaux de Richard Schwartz |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/268676793_Dynamiser_la_geometrie_elementaire_introduction_a_des_travaux_de_Richard_Schwartz |journal=[[Rendiconti di Matematica e delle sue Applicazioni]] |volume=25 |issue=VII |pages=127-153 |via=ResearchGate}}</ref> and he has been credited for developing the mathematical concept known as the [[pentagram map]].<ref name="twsZA28" /> In addition, he is author of a mathematics picture book for young children.<ref name="twsZA17">{{cite news
 |title= Top 10/Top5/Editor's Picks/Editor's Note
 |newspaper= Brown Daily Herald
 |date= February 3, 2011
 |url= http://post.browndailyherald.com/2011/02/03/top-10top5editors-pickseditors-note/
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> In 2018 he is a professor of mathematics at [[Brown University]].

==Career==
Schwartz was born in [[Los Angeles, California|Los Angeles]] on August 11, 1966. He attended [[John F. Kennedy High School (Los Angeles)|John F. Kennedy High School]] in Los Angeles from 1981 to 1984, then earned a [[Bachelor's degree|B. S.]] in [[mathematics]] from [[University of California, Los Angeles|U.C.L.A.]] in 1987, and then a [[Doctorate|Ph. D.]] in [[mathematics]] from [[Princeton University]] in 1991 under the supervision of [[William Thurston]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=18909|title = Richard Schwartz - the Mathematics Genealogy Project}}</ref> He taught at the [[University of Maryland]]. He is currently the Chancellor's Professor of Mathematics at [[Brown University]]. He lives with his wife and two daughters in [[Barrington, Rhode Island]].

Schwartz is credited by other mathematicians for introducing the concept of the [[pentagram map]].<ref name=twsZA28>{{cite journal
 |author= Fedor Soloviev
 |title= Integrability of the pentagram map
 |journal= Duke Mathematical Journal
 |quote= The pentagram map was introduced by R. Schwartz in 1992 for convex planar polygons
 |date= June 27, 2011
 |volume= 162
 |issue= 15
 |doi= 10.1215/00127094-2382228
 |arxiv= 1106.3950
 |s2cid= 119586878
 }}</ref>
According to Schwartz's conception, a convex polygon would be inscribed with diagonal lines inside it, by drawing a line from one point to the next point—that is, by skipping over the immediate point on the polygon. The intersection points of the diagonals would form an inner polygon, and the process could be repeated.<ref name=twsZA24>{{cite journal
| last1=Glick | first1=Max
| title=The pentagram map and Y-patterns
| journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]
| volume=227 | issue=2 | date=1 June 2011 | pages=1019-1045
| doi=10.1016/j.aim.2011.02.018 | doi-access=free
| quote= The pentagram map, introduced by R. Schwartz, is defined by the following construction: given a polygon as input, draw all of its "shortest" diagonals, and output the smaller polygon which they cut out. We employ the machinery of cluster algebras to obtain explicit formulas for the iterates of the pentagram map. 
| arxiv=1005.0598}}</ref> Schwartz observed these geometric patterns, partly by experimenting with computers.<ref name=twsZA23>{{cite news
 |author1=Richard Evan Schwartz |author2=Serge Tabachnikov |title=The Pentagram Integrals on Inscribed Polygons
 |publisher= Mendeley
 |year= 2010
 |url= http://www.mendeley.com/research/pentagram-integrals-inscribed-polygons-7/
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> 
He has collaborated with mathematicians Valentin Ovsienko<ref name=twsZA26>{{cite news
 |author= V Ovsienko
 |title= The Pentagram map: a discrete integrable system
 |publisher= University of Cambridge
 |quote= (academic lecture by mathematician V Ovsienko on the pentagram map subject)
 |date= 2011-06-27
 |url= http://www.sms.cam.ac.uk/media/536614
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> 
and [[Sergei Tabachnikov]]<ref name=twsZA21>{{cite journal
 |author1=Valentin Ovsienko |author2=Richard Schwartz |author3=Serge Tabachnikov |title= The Pentagram Map: A Discrete Integrable System
 |doi= 10.1007/s00220-010-1075-y 
 |pages= 409–446
 |year= 2010
 |url= http://academic.research.microsoft.com/Publication/5128335/the-pentagram-map-a-discrete-integrable-system
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
 |volume=299
 |issue=2 |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics
|arxiv=0810.5605|bibcode=2010CMaPh.299..409O|s2cid=2616239 }}</ref> 
to show that the pentagram map is "completely integrable."<ref name=twsZA22>{{cite journal
 |author1=Valentin Ovsienko |title=Discrete monodromy, pentagrams, and the method of condensation |journal=Journal of Fixed Point Theory and Applications |author2=Richard Schwartz |author3=Serge Tabachnikov |publisher= Springerlink
 |date= 2011-06-27
 |doi=10.1007/s11784-008-0079-0
 |volume=3
 |issue=2 |pages=379–409
|arxiv=0709.1264|s2cid=17099073 }}</ref>

In his spare time he draws [[comic book]]s,<ref name=twsZA15/> writes computer programs, listens to [[music]] and exercises. He admired the late [[Russia]]n mathematician [[Vladimir Arnold]] and dedicated a paper to him.<ref name=twsZA22/> He played an [[April Fool's joke]] on fellow mathematics professors at Brown University by sending an email suggesting that students could be admitted randomly, along with references to bogus studies which purportedly suggested that there were benefits to having a certain population of the student body selected at random; the story was reported in the ''[[Brown Daily Herald]]''.<ref name=twsZA16>{{cite news
 |title= Merit blind admissions fool math profs on April 1st.
 |newspaper= Brown Daily Herald
 |date= April 17, 2008
 |url= http://www.browndailyherald.com/features/merit-blind-admissions-fool-math-profs-on-april-1-1.1670332
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> Colleagues such as mathematician Jeffrey Brock describe Schwartz as having a "very wry sense of humor."<ref name=twsZA16/>

In 2003, Schwartz was teaching one of his young daughters about number basics and developed a poster of the first 100 numbers using colorful monsters. This project gelled into a mathematics book for young children published in 2010, entitled ''You Can Count on Monsters'', which became a bestseller.<ref name=twsZA15/> Each monster has a graphic which gives a mini-lesson about its properties, such as being a [[prime number]] or a lesson about [[factorization|factoring]]; for example, the graphic monster for the number five was a five-sided star or [[pentagram]].<ref name=twsZA15/>  A year after publication, it was featured prominently on ''[[National Public Radio]]'' in January 2011 and became a bestseller for a few days on the online bookstore [[Amazon.com|Amazon]]<ref name=twsZA15/> as well as earning international acclaim.<ref name=twsZA13>{{cite news
 |author= PRNewsWire News Releases
 |title= You Can Count on Monsters Proclaimed a Self-Learning Tool That Makes Math Fun
 |newspaper= Boston Globe
 |quote= You Can Count on Monsters, a creatively educational children's book that illustrates prime and composite numbers through colorful monsters-themed geometrical designs, has earned international acclaim and stellar sales since its January debut on NPR's Weekend Edition. 
 |date= March 21, 2011
 |url= http://finance.boston.com/boston/news/read?GUID=17856440
 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111004225908/http://finance.boston.com/boston/news/read?GUID=17856440
 |url-status= dead
 |archive-date= October 4, 2011
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> 
The ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' suggested that the book helped to "take the scariness out of arithmetic."<ref name=twsZA12>{{cite news
 |title= Summer reading: Children's books
 |newspaper= Los Angeles Times
 |date= May 22, 2011
 |url= https://www.latimes.com/books/la-xpm-2011-may-22-la-ca-summer-childrens-20110522-story.html
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> 
Mathematician Keith Devlin, on ''NPR'', agreed, saying that Schwartz "very skillfully and subtly embeds mathematical ideas into the drawings."
<ref name=twsZA11>{{cite news
 |author= NPR Staff
 |title= Math Isn't So Scary With Help From These Monsters
 |publisher= NPR
 |date= January 22, 2011
 |url= https://www.npr.org/2011/01/22/133118069/math-isnt-so-scary-with-help-from-these-monsters
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref> 
<ref name=twsZA15>{{cite news
 |author= Ben Kutner
 |title= Math and monsters add up in children's book
 |newspaper= Brown Daily Herald
 |date= February 2, 2011
 |url= http://www.browndailyherald.com/math-and-monsters-add-up-in-children-s-book-1.2455113
 |access-date= 2011-06-27
}}</ref>

==Publications==

===Selected contributions===
*The [[quasi-isometry]] classification of rank one lattices: Any quasi-isometry of a [[hyperbolic space|hyperbolic]] lattice is equivalent to a [[commensurator]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Schwartz | first1=Richard Evan
| title=The quasi-isometry classification of rank one lattices
| date=1995
| journal=[[Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS]]
| volume=82 | pages=133-168
| doi=10.1007/BF02698639 | doi-access=free}}</ref>
*A proof of the 1989 [[William Goldman (mathematician)|Goldman]]–Parker conjecture: This is a complete description of the [[moduli space]] of the complex hyperbolic ideal triangle groups.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Schwartz | first1=Richard Evan
| title=Ideal Triangle Groups, Dented Tori, and Numerical Analysis
| date=2001
| journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]
| volume=153 | issue=3 | pages=533-598
| doi=10.2307/2661362}}</ref>
*A proof that a [[triangle]] has a periodic [[Dynamical billiards|billiard]] path provided all its angles are less than 100 degrees.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Schwartz | first1=Richard Evan
| title=Obtuse triangular billiards II: one hundred degrees worth of periodic trajectories
| date=2009
| journal=[[Experimental Mathematics (journal)|Experimental Mathematics]]
| volume=18 | issue=2 | pages=137-171
| doi=10.1080/10586458.2009.10128891}}</ref>
*A solution of the 1960 [[Jürgen Moser|Moser]]–[[Bernard Neumann|Neumann]] problem: There exists an [[outer billiard]]s system with an unbounded orbit.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Schwartz | first1=Richard Evan
| title=Unbounded orbits for Outer Billiards
| date=2007
| journal=Journal of Modern Dynamics
| volume=1 | issue=3 | pages=371-424
| doi=10.3934/jmd.2007.1.371}}</ref>
*A solution of the 5-[[electron]] case of [[J. J. Thomson]]'s 1904 [[Thomson problem|problem]]: The [[triangular bipyramid]] is the configuration of 5 electrons on the [[sphere]] that minimizes the [[Coulomb potential]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Schwartz | first1=Richard Evan
| title=The five-electron case of Thomson’s problem
| date=2013
| journal=[[Experimental Mathematics (journal)|Experimental Mathematics]]
| volume=22 | issue=2 | pages=157-186
| doi=10.1080/10586458.2013.766570}}</ref>
*The introduction of the [[pentagram map]]<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Schwartz | first1=Richard Evan
| title=The pentagram map
| date=1992
| journal=[[Experimental Mathematics (journal)|Experimental Mathematics]]
| volume=1 | issue=1 | pages=71-81
| url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/experimental-mathematics/volume-1/issue-1/The-pentagram-map/em/1048709118.full}}</ref> and a later proof (with Valentin Ovsienko and Sergei Tabachnikov) of its complete [[Integrable system|integrability]].<ref name=twsZA21/>

==Selected awards==
*1993 [[National Science Foundation]] Postdoctoral Fellow
*1996 [[Sloan Research Fellow]]
*2002 Invited Speaker, [[International Congress of Mathematicians]], Beijing
*2003 [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]]
*2009 [[Clay Mathematics Institute|Clay Research Scholar]]
*2017 class of [[Fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]] "for contributions to dynamics, geometry, and experimental mathematics and for exposition".<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/ams-fellows/new-fellows 2017 Class of the Fellows of the AMS], [[American Mathematical Society]], retrieved 2016-11-06.</ref>
In June 2026, the conference "''Geometry, Dynamics, and Computer-Assisted Proofs''" is held in his honor at [[Heidelberg University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Geometry, Dynamics, and Computer-Assisted Proofs |url=https://sites.google.com/view/rich-problems/main-page |access-date=2026-06-19 |website=sites.google.com |language=en-US}}</ref>
